name: Adapalene

lead: Adapalene is a synthetic third-generation topical retinoid developed for acne vulgaris. It became the first retinoid sold over the counter for acne in the United States in 2016 (as a 0.1% gel), following earlier prescription availability, and is also marketed in combination with benzoyl peroxide or clindamycin.

Beyond acne it is used off-label for texture, keratosis pilaris and some signs of photoaging. Many users describe it as the most accessible retinoid, since it can be bought without a prescription and is reported to cause less irritation than tretinoin.

paras: Adapalene selectively activates retinoic acid receptors beta and gamma, which normalizes follicular keratinocyte differentiation, prevents microcomedone formation and has direct anti-inflammatory effects. It is chemically more stable than tretinoin and less affected by light and benzoyl peroxide, which makes it easy to combine with other acne actives.

Initial dryness, redness, burning and peeling are common and typically peak in the first few weeks. Photosensitivity is reported, and daily sunscreen is generally advised. Use in pregnancy is generally discouraged despite reassuring limited human data. Benefits take about 8 to 12 weeks to appear, and combining with other irritants can worsen tolerability.

lead: Adapalene, sold under the brand name Differin among others, is a third-generation synthetic topical retinoid used mainly for mild to moderate acne vulgaris. It is used off-label for keratosis pilaris and has been explored for photoaging and other conditions [1]. Since 2016 a 0.1 percent adapalene gel has been available over the counter in the United States, the first formerly prescription-only retinoid to be sold that way for acne [1].

Guidelines list topical retinoids, with adapalene the principal example in UK guidance, as first-line acne treatment, either alone or with benzoyl peroxide or an antibiotic [2][3][4]. A systematic review of 54 trials of US-approved topical retinoids found them superior to vehicle on investigator global assessments [5].

Wikipedia describes adapalene as often regarded as the best tolerated of the three topical retinoids, with less irritation than tretinoin, and as chemically more stable, so that it can be used with benzoyl peroxide and is less affected by light [1]. Typical adverse effects are dryness, redness, burning and peeling in the first weeks, and photosensitivity [1][6].
infobox: Differin; also combinations with benzoyl peroxide and with clindamycin
Galderma (patented 1986 in Luxembourg, 1988 in the US)
Not well studied; US combination label lists Pregnancy Category C

paras: Retinoids such as adapalene are first-line acne therapy under recommendations of the Global Alliance to Improve Outcomes in Acne, used alone or with benzoyl peroxide and an antimicrobial such as clindamycin; fixed combinations with benzoyl peroxide, and with benzoyl peroxide plus clindamycin, are available [1]. The 2024 American Academy of Dermatology guideline strongly recommends topical retinoids and benzoyl peroxide, and advises combining topical therapies with different mechanisms [2]. A UK review notes that guidelines differ over whether benzoyl peroxide or a topical retinoid, mainly adapalene, should be the lead agent, and that treatments take 6 to 8 weeks to work [4].
The US label for adapalene 0.1 percent with benzoyl peroxide 2.5 percent gel indicates it for acne vulgaris in patients 9 years and older [6].

Because adapalene reduces keratinocyte differentiation and keratin deposition, Wikipedia notes use for keratosis pilaris and callus. Other reported off-label uses include warts, molluscum contagiosum, Darier's disease, photoaging, pigmentary disorders and actinic keratoses [1]. A systematic review of perioral dermatitis lists adapalene gel among treatment options that need further research [7]. Outside acne, adapalene is sold over the counter only at 0.1 percent; oleyl adapalenate is a different ingredient marketed for broader cosmetic skincare [1].

Adapalene is highly lipophilic and readily penetrates hair follicles. It binds nuclear retinoic acid receptors, chiefly beta and gamma subtypes, and through the retinoid X receptor modulates keratinocyte proliferation and differentiation; this normalises follicular keratinization, reduces microcomedone formation and increases cell turnover. It is also described as anti-inflammatory, suppressing responses to Cutibacterium acnes and inhibiting lipoxygenase activity [1]. Per Wikipedia, adding an RAR-gamma antagonist removes its clinical efficacy, suggesting gamma agonism drives its action [1]. The US label states that its exact role in acne has not been established beyond effects on differentiation, keratinization and inflammation [6].

Skin absorption is low. In one study of six acne patients, plasma levels were below 0.35 ng/mL after daily application, and trials of chronic users found about 0.25 ng/mL. About a quarter of the drug is metabolised, mostly to glucuronides, and the rest is excreted unchanged [1]. A registered phase 4 study compared systemic exposure of 0.3 percent and 0.1 percent gels in 51 patients [8].

The 2019 systematic review of 54 trials found topical retinoids superior to vehicle, with improvements of 24.1 to 28.8 percent on the Investigator Global Assessment and 13.3 to 17.3 percent on the Static Global Assessment, and larger improvements when combined with benzoyl peroxide [5]. Wikipedia reports that studies have found adapalene about as effective as other retinoids with less irritation [1].
A phase 2 fixed-dose triple combination of clindamycin 1.2 percent, benzoyl peroxide 3.1 percent and adapalene 0.15 percent was tested in moderate-to-severe acne [9][10].

Between 1 and 10 percent of users experience brief warmth or stinging, dryness, peeling and redness in the first two to four weeks; this retinoid reaction is often called retinization and tends to resolve within about four weeks of once-daily use [1]. The US combination label lists dry skin, contact dermatitis, application-site burning and irritation as the most common events (at least 1 percent), and advises sunscreen and avoiding sunlight [6].

Topical adapalene in pregnancy has not been well studied, with a theoretical risk of retinoid embryopathy, and no evidence so far of harm; low blood levels suggest low risk to nursing infants [1]. The US combination label states that there are no well-controlled trials in pregnant women [6]. Trials of ceramide-containing moisturizers alongside anti-acne treatment have aimed at reducing irritation and improving adherence [11][12].

Acne: a registered phase 3 efficacy and safety study of adapalene 0.1 percent enrolled 1,075 patients; a 753-patient study compared adapalene 0.3 percent gel with Differin and placebo; and a 601-patient bioequivalence study was run in acne patients [13][14][15]. A compound adapalene and clindamycin gel was studied in 245 patients [16].
Photoaging: a phase 3 comparison of adapalene 0.3 percent gel with tretinoin 0.05 percent emollient cream for photoaging enrolled 128 participants [17].
Acne scars: a small phase 2 study (20 participants) tested adapalene 0.3 percent gel in atrophic acne scars [18].

Tolerability and combinations: phase 1 studies compared Differin cream with lotion in healthy skin (75 and 69 participants), a phase 3 trial tested a moisturizer with licochalcone A alongside adapalene gel in 120 acne patients, and phase 2 and 3 trials tested the triple-combination gel [19][20][21][9].

Adapalene came out of research at the Swiss company Galderma, was patented in Luxembourg in 1986 and in the US in 1988, and was approved by the US FDA as a prescription acne medication in 1996. In 2016 the FDA approved the 0.1 percent gel for over-the-counter sale, the first time a formerly prescription-only retinoid became available without prescription for acne [1]. Wikipedia also notes research interest in adapalene for plantar warts and, in a computational study, as a possible SARS-CoV-2 entry inhibitor [1].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org adapalene is usually discussed as the over-the-counter alternative to prescription tretinoin, while T Nation posters over many years mention Differin gel in threads about acne on the face, back and shoulders.
